say.text: Safar, 549 AH: April, 1154. Nur ad-Din entered Damascus, having pledged to respect the lives and the property of its people.
He besieged Mujir ad-Din in the citadel and wrote to him, offering a great fief, with the city of Homs in it. Mujir ad-Din accepted, left the citadel and went to Homs.
The Franks, who had been gathering to relieve the city, heard that it had fallen to Nur ad-Din, and went home.
Let no one be harmed who is not armed against us. That is the word I gave at the gate, and the word is the city's now.
Ibn al-Athir, who wrote the Zengid house's history and admired Nur ad-Din, says that he treated the people of Damascus with the greatest consideration and ruled them with perfect justice.
Nur ad-Din was just and pious, and built colleges across Syria, and in Damascus a hospital and a school for the study of Tradition.
Salah ad-Din, who had grown up in his father's care, stayed in Nur ad-Din's service. Nur ad-Din advanced him, and admitted him among his friends.
Ibn Khallikan judged that it was from Nur ad-Din that he learned righteousness, and zeal in the war against the Franks.
You kept your head. That is more than I did at your age.
I kept my head because you stood where I could see you, uncle.
